title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
content:
Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide. I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application.

You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io:

  • Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script
  • Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI
  • Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository
  • Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette
  • Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools

The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo.

As an example, consider the following URL:

https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this:

That's Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table.

Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing:

https://lite.datasette.io/
  ?install=datasette-maplibre
  &url=https://.../demo.db
  &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml
  #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=... as many times as you like to load more plugins.

&url=https://.../demo.db loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers - I host files like this in Gists, because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file.

&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file. The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file.

#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it (%23 is a URL-encoded #) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent column in the data.

That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments last year.

The full set of supported URL arguments is described in the Datasette Lite README.

I've already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here's a recent issue describing a pagination bug - I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite:

Demo of the bug: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score - click next and the second page is empty.

Here's that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43): https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score

How this works, using service workers

Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022, originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value.

The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack. It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML.

This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML don't execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files.

The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers. These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead.

Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this:

/app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML)
/app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML)
/app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript)
/app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS)

Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a /app/aa94e6851595/ prefix. What's that about?

The /app/<session>/ prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs.

Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the datasette-maplibre plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another.

The service worker for lite.datasette.io is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure.

Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session.

(We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!)

I had Claude Fable 5.2 generate several SVG diagrams to help explain this. Here's my favorite of those, now embedded in the Datasette Lite README:

This system started life back in May as an AI research spike generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn't until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production!

Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLite

I added this feature last night as an off-shoot of investigating a potential bug in SQLite.

Datasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then.

Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues.

In the past I've used various tricks to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it's not a trivial process.

WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab.

datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels is my new repository which contains WebAssembly compiled Python wheels for pysqlite3 for 163 different SQLite versions. Each version gets a file with a name like this:

pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl

That's for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version.

Datasette Lite now takes a special ?sqlite= URL parameter, which will accept a version number like 3.54.1, resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it.

Once I'd built the wheels, I decided to have Claude Fable 5.2 build me [this bonus tool](https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29) for comparing a SQL query across any selected versions of SQLite. Here's an example showing how select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) differs between SQLite 3.54.0 and 3.54.1:

This should work for every other Python app, too

Nothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick - running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs.

C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can even publish them to PyPI as of PEP 783 in April 2026.

One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden.

I'd love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem.

title: SetShot 1.0 (and a Personal Tale of Defaults System Spelunking)
content:
Adam Engst, writing at TidBITS:

This past August, I did something I had never done before: released a full-fledged Mac app. Prompted by tech ghost stories about settings mysteriously changing during operating system updates, I spent months working with Claude Code to create a utility called SetShot that would reveal what settings change during macOS updates (see “SetShot Tracks macOS Settings Changes,” 19 August 2026). So far, I haven’t caught Apple red-handed, although I still hear chatter about configuration changes after users install updates.

Practically speaking, SetShot offers something never previously available to Mac users: the capability to identify and log settings changes over time, whether made by you, macOS, or some app. To that end, it takes and compares snapshots of numerous settings deep within macOS, reporting on what changed between them. It never changes any settings, so the worst it can do is tell you something you didn’t want to know.

SetShot is a very cool app, and so very Adam Engst-flavored. Free of charge and open source to boot.

There’s an anecdote involving me in Engst’s post, and while SetShot couldn’t fix my problem directly, it was very helpful in showing me where to look to fix it myself. The backstory: I set a custom “Text highlight color” in System Preferences: Appearances many years ago — I mean like maybe 20 years ago — and had not changed it in years. It’s just the perfect shade of blue. But one night two months ago I went screwing around to see what the modern default text highlight colors are, and, son of a bitch, when I tried to change my color back to the custom one I’d been using for decades, I couldn’t. The way the color picker stores color values from the modern Appearance settings panel must have changed. It still honors the old value I had if it’s in the defaults system that way, but it writes a different style of value if you change it in the Appearance panel in System Settings.

Here’s a short version of how I got my old color back. Using System Settings, I changed the custom color to the exact RGB values 0.2 / 0.4 / 0.6. Then I read them from the command line:

❯ defaults read -g AppleHighlightColor
0.200000 0.400000 0.600000 Other

That’s not the color I wanted; I just wanted to prove that that’s the global key for a custom text highlight color. When I read those same values from a backup version of my ~/Library/Preferences/.GlobalPreferences.plist file (always have backups, kids), with my beloved custom color, it looked liked this:

❯ defaults read /path/to/.GlobalPreferences.plist AppleHighlightColor
0.698039 0.760784 0.835294

So the old value was a string with three floating point RGB values. The new value was a string with those three values plus the word “Other”. This command, writing back my custom RGB values without the word “Other”:

❯ defaults write -g AppleHighlightColor "0.698039 0.760784 0.835294"

restored the color I’ve been using since George W. Bush was still president. It’s a really good color, trust me.

Remembrance of proteins past (permalink)

Without a doubt, the best piece of media from the 2026 midterms was Scott Colom's "Pick another senator instead" ad from his triumphant Mississippi senate campaign against GOP incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith:

https://youtu.be/zpUnm09lTUk?si=3ApbHida5_VpQCLB&t=2219

Some background: Colom is the first Black Mississippi senator elected since Reconstruction gave way to Jim Crow. He's also the first Democratic Mississippi senator since 1982. Colom's campaign shifted the statewide vote leftward by 19 points, and he won a quarter of the state's white votes.

Colom ran a great campaign and promoted great policies, but also: he ran one of the great political ads of all time. That ad skewered Hyde-Smith's "let them eat whey powder" remark to WLOX Biloxi host Hugh Keeton, who asked her about the cost of living crisis and the high price of beef, to which she replied that people "have so many proteins to choose from":

https://www.mississippifreepress.org/americans-who-cant-afford-beef-have-so-many-proteins-to-choose-from-says-us-sen-cindy-hyde-smith/

Colom's ad plays a montage of Mississippians expressing disgust with Hyde-Smith's response, saying "I'd rather choose another senator instead." Colom was quick to credit content creator Ryan Sayles, who joined the campaign after doing some freelance work for them, as the ad's mastermind:

https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/12/ryan-sayles-scott-colom-viral-protein-ad-01163508

Much has been said about the ad's style, especially the viral "s-h-e-e-e-i-t" voiced by US Army vet Russ Hudson, who stepped in to do the ad when his father declined to curse on camera:

https://edition.cnn.com/2026/11/15/politics/scott-colom-viral-protein-ad-mississippi-senate

But the most important analysis on the ad is of its substance, specifically how it repudiates one of the key doctrines of neoliberal, austerity economics, as David Dayen writes for The American Prospect:

https://prospect.org/2026/11/16/how-the-mississippi-senate-win-exposed-austerity-logic/

Neoliberalism is the signature achievement of the "law and economics" movement that came out of the University of Chicago. The central conceit of law and econ is that economics is a "hard science" (not a social science) and that its domain is a deterministic, quantifiable physics of human behavior. Economists went so far as to create a fake "Nobel Prize" in economics in a bid to elevate their work out of the social sciences:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/09/18/falsifiability/#figleaves-not-rubrics

This "science" claims it can replace squishy, qualitative questions with mathematical models that can output the objectively correct answer to every thorny political question, thereby substituting an obscure form of mathematics for political deliberation:

https://pluralistic.net/2023/04/03/all-models-are-wrong/#some-are-useful

This is a remarkably cheap and transparent stunt. To produce this "mathematics of human behavior," you must first quantize all the qualitative questions so that they can be plugged into variables in econ equations. But here's the problem: assigning a numeric value to a qualitative factor is a qualitative exercise!

When an economist decides that the pain you'll experience as a result of their policy prescriptions is worth "7" while the benefit is worth "8," they are not doing objective work, they're just declaring their own judgments (and biases) to be empirical observations, while demoting your judgments to mere "feelings" (and biases):

https://pluralistic.net/2024/09/18/falsifiability/#figleaves-not-rubrics

Economism doesn't just eliminate qualitative questions from policymaking: it incinerates all of those qualitative factors so that economists can perform mathematics on whatever dubious quantitative residue remains in the crucible:

https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-qualia/

This is where Scott Colom's brilliant campaign ad comes in. As Dayen points out, when Hyde-Smith made her "many other proteins to choose from," gaffe, she was referencing a key piece of economic theory that has been thoroughly weaponized by the neoliberals: "substitution."

On its face, substitution is just the commonsense proposition that when prices for one good or service go up, some consumers will substitute another. When gas prices go up, more people ride the bus. When Instagram increases its ad-load, more people switch to Mastodon or Bluesky. When your ISP jacks up your price, you might switch to another carrier.

So far, so good. Indeed, one of the best things about digital products and services is how low digital "switching costs" (the cost you bear when switching from one service to another) can be. The lower the switching costs are, the easier it is to substitute one thing for another.

This means that, in a state of nature, tech bosses have to be careful about enshittifying their products, lest their users defect to a rival. This is why tech bosses have spent decades doing everything they can to jack up those "switching costs." They want to convert all their users into hostages:

https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2021/08/facebooks-secret-war-switching-costs

Substitution is real and it makes sense. The problem comes when neoliberal economists use this idea in policy. In the early 2010s, Barack Obama proposed applying substitution to the American welfare system through something called "Chained CPI."

"CPI" stands for the "Consumer Price Index": this is a measurement of the cost of a "basket of goods" (a bunch of supposedly representative household items) that is used to make inflationary adjustments to a variety of payments. When the CPI goes up, so do social security, welfare and disability payments. Otherwise, inflation would continually reduce the living standards of everyone who receives these entitlements.

"Chained CPI" takes the CPI and applies substitution to it. Rather than asking whether hamburger just got more expensive, the economists who calculate CPI ask whether the cheapest protein at the grocery store got more expensive (because hamburger can be swapped out for another protein).

Chained CPI's intent and effect is to reduce payments to retirees, disabled people, and poor people. Chained CPI is always going to be lower than CPI, because chained CPI only rises when the cheapest "substitute" for one of the items in CPI's "basket of goods" gets more expensive. In effect, the "basket of goods" becomes a transdimensional basket, one that contains every substitute good that might have gone into the basket in all possible parallel universes. Economists get to universe-shop for the dimension where that basket has the lowest cost, and then we all have to live in their chosen universe.

Obama tried to adopt it 2013 as part of a "grand bargain" to reduce the deficit, but was thwarted by the Tea Party Caucus, who refused the grand bargain on the grounds that it contained an infinitesimal tax rise for the richest Americans:

https://abcnews.com/blogs/politics/2013/04/obamas-chained-cpi-throws-off-pols-and-heres-how-it-works/

But chained CPI is one of the most cherished ideas of neoliberal thinktanks, so it came back in 2017 for Trump's tax giveaway to the super-rich, whose costs were partially offset by using chained CPI to calculate tax brackets, the standard deduction, and the Earned Income Tax Credit:

https://newrepublic.com/article/145688/biggest-trojan-horse-republican-tax-plan

As Dayen writes, "[This created] a regressive tax increase by eroding deductions and credits and pushing people into higher tax brackets. The wealthy were unaffected by this since they were already in the highest tax bracket and itemized rather than using the standard deduction."

Which brings me back to Cindy Hyde-Smith's foot-in-mouth remarks about "so many proteins." Whether or not Hyde-Smith knew it, she was referencing this substitution/chained CPI doctrine when she told people that beef inflation didn't matter because other proteins were available. In doing so, she was performing economism's cheapest trick: pretending that her opinions are objective facts, while other people's opinions are just feelings.

As Dayen writes, "[W]ho decides whether the cheaper product they switch to is 'similar' to the one that’s become so expensive that the consumer must give it up?…The logic is, approximately: You're not doing as badly as you think, so pick another protein and quit your whining."

People do substitute one thing for another as a matter of economic necessity. But the idea that a "substitute" is an "equivalent" can only be accepted if you first buy into the economist's conceit that all qualitative matters can be safely incinerated, leaving the expert to do math on the quantitative ash.

In this conceit, if you can't afford hamburgers and end up substituting chicken or fish, then you've found a new protein and have lost no "welfare." If you think otherwise, then you are expressing an irrational preference (unlike economists, whose preference for having a Nobel prize of their own is so empirically correct that it could be detected by a Martian peering at Earth through a telescope).

It's not only Cindy Hyde-Smith who unconsciously metabolized the idea of substitution as "rationality"; it's the voters, too, who recognized in Hyde-Smith's remarks the arrogance of policy elites who've spent decades discounting their views as "feelings" while declaring their own views to be experimental validated facts. Not only do voters recognize this move: they hate it.

They know that elites are perfectly capable of expressing strong views about qualitative matters and moving heaven and Earth to achieve a life that fits with their aesthetics. They know that the same Ivy League economists who dismiss their preferences as "irrational" will revel for 4,000 pages' worth of Marcel Proust expounding on the spiritual, intangible reasons for choosing his favorite baked goods.

Economics is the study of why people do things, but somewhere along the way it became a club used to force people to do the things that powerful people prefer. The (alleged) "rationalism" of economism has worn out its welcome. You don't need an economics degree to understand why that "rationalism" is a cheap trick: after 50 years of neoliberalism, a Martian with a telescope could spot it.

title: HomeAssistant - shrink a HAOS qcow2 filesystem
content:
Mostly notes to myself, I hope they're helpful to you too!

My HomeAssistant OS (HAOS) was originally thinly provisioned with a 30GB virtual disk stored in a qcow2 file. In theory, the file should only take up as much space as the virtual filesystem. In reality, it grows to accommodate the maximum size allowed.

My HAOS was showing only 10GB used:

But running ls -lh showed 32GB was allocated. To see the actual space on disk, I ran du -h haos.qcow2 which showed 28GB.

As it is 2026, I can't afford to simply buy a few more TB of SSD, so here's how to manually shrink the file so it only takes up the space it needs.

  1. Within HomeAssistant's web interface, completely shut down.
    • Settings → ⋮ → Restart Home Assistant → More options → Shut Down System
    • Wait a few minutes for everything to finish shutting down.
  2. Within your host Operating System, backup your existing file!
    • sudo cp haos.qcow2 haos.qcow2.bak
  3. Check the size of the disk:
    • sudo qemu-img info haos.qcow2
  4. Shrink (sparsify) the disk.
    • sudo virt-sparsify --in-place haos.qcow2
    • This may take a few moments.
  5. Check the size of the disk to make sure it has shrunk:
    • sudo qemu-img info haos.qcow2
  6. Once that has finished, you can start the virtual machine again.
    • virsh list --all to find the name of the VM.
    • virsh start haos
  7. Wait a few minutes and your HomeAssistant should come back to life. If all is well, you can delete the backup.
    • sudo rm haos.qcow2.bak

There doesn't seem to be an automated way to do this. If you do know a way to make this easier - please leave a comment in the box.

title: Stacked diffs with Maiao
content:
I have been using the community fork of Maiao for a little while now, and it is excellent. For anyone who prefers working with stacked diffs, but needs to interact with a more traditional forge such as GitHub, try using Maiao for a bit. It just does the right thing in almost every situation. It’s cut my frustration with GitHub at least in half, if not more.

For the small group of readers who are stoked about stacked diffs, that’s probably enough of a pitch. For the rest of the world, let’s back up a little.

On traditional forge platforms, pre-commit code review happens on pull requests (sometimes called merge requests), where each pull request is created from a git branch.

Users that are new to git can then think of a branch as one development effort toward a small goal. They keep adding commits to that branch as long as its tip does not represent the goal state. At the end, when everything looks right and the change is approved, they perform an explicit merge. This means they create a merge commit on the upstream branch that references both the old upstream and the branch they worked on.

title: The NVIDIA Bubble
content:
If you liked this piece, you should subscribe to my premium newsletter, and you can subscribe on the following links: $70 a year, $18 a quarter, or $7 a month.

In return, you get a weekly premium newsletter that dives deep into the finances of the AI bubble. Over the past few months, I’ve published a two part guide to the world of AI debt, an analysis of the (dubious) impact of generative AI on the global economy, deep analyses of the biggest players in the AI infrastructure space like NVIDIA (part one and two) and Oracle (part one and two), and the role private credit is playing in funding AI data centers, and how private equity, reeling from years of successive failed software acquisitions, is doubling down on the AI bubble. 

Last week’s piece was a 13,000-word deep dive into Megaspeed — the shady firm at the heart of Jensen’s downfall, which somehow bought billions of GPUs despite being, just a few years ago, an unsuccessful developer of free-to-play mobile games. It’s all very weird, and I spent a lot of time making sense of it all. 

On Friday, I’m going to share how we fix the tech industry, and how we stop the next bubble before it even starts.  

If you want to get in touch — and especially if you have any juicy information about Anthropic, OpenAI, or any other companies in the AI bubble — hit me up on Signal at ezitron.76. I’m also on IB on your Bloomberg Terminal. 

This weekend, thousands of horrible little men cried out for the return of their pervert emperor, demanding that NVIDIA restore disgraced CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned after it leaked that he’d had multiple affairs, one of which (as described in my free newsletter last week) was with a woman called Alice Huang who may or may not have been a Chinese spy, but was most certainly selling restricted AI chips to Chinese companies through a company called Megaspeed (covered in depth in my premium last week). 

Within the space of a week, illegal chip sales routed through Alice Huang’s empire went from $4.8 billion to “at least” $7.5 billion, to $12 billion between March 2024 and June 2025 according to the Wall Street Journal. 

The Information also reported that companies connected to Alice Huang invested in DeepSeek, the famed Chinese AI lab that spooked the world back in Q1 2025 for, ironically, suggesting that we didn’t need to buy as many NVIDIA GPUs.

Let’s be clear about something: Jensen Huang resigned and is not coming back. To paraphrase Semafor’s Rohan Goswami, NVIDIA’s board was packed with allies, deliberated at length about what to do (and didn’t really want to do it), and has both let him walk and done nothing to retain him, I’d personally guess because the probe the board is running already has some idea of wrongdoing such as, I dunno, the giant illegal smuggling ring that has been covered at length by basically every media outlet. NVIDIA has also said it was not considering bringing him back.

Even now, a week into this bizarre crisis, few are truly reconciling with the allegations raised in May 2026 by Culper Research’s short report, namely that 20% or more ($43bn+) of NVIDIA’s FY 2026 sales came from selling through China. Even two profiles of Culper in the New York Times and Wall Street Journal fail to substantively discuss the material of the guy they’re god damn profiling.

That’s because, to paraphrase Culper’s own work, Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg. As I covered last week, Culper directly connects Megaspeed to popular AI server manufacturer Supermicro, whose co-founder and board member Wally Liaw was arrested with several co-conspirators back in March for trying to sell over $2.5 billion in chips to a Chinese passthrough entity Culper believes is a Megaspeed affiliate. Liaw had previously resigned in 2018 due to an accounting scandal (per short seller Hindenburg), only to be rehired in 2021 as a consultant and reinstated to the board in 2023.

Let me spell it out for you: a co-founder and member of the board of one of the largest manufacturers of AI servers was arrested for selling chips to China, specifically to a company affiliated with the very same smuggling operation that Alice Huang ran. 

Supermicro is a huge, publicly-listed company with a history of accounting scandals. 70% or more of its revenues come from selling AI servers powered by NVIDIA GPUs, and back in August 2024 — months into Megaspeed’s $12 billion purchases of eventually-smuggled GPUs — Supermicro was NVIDIA’s third-largest customer, around that it was facing allegations of accounting manipulation and sanction evasion by Hindenburg that never went anywhere because our markets are broken and our SEC is trash.

Anyway, my point is that this story is just getting started, and that those in the Copium dens are trying to reframe this as a “guy who made a mistake” rather than a philanderer that appears to have overseen the GPU equivalent of Iran Contra. Whatever rumors you may have read about a potential Jensen comeback appear to be peddled by the most desperate of AI boosters who, based on reports on CNBC, do not appear to be aligned with what Huang himself has said. 

And really, why do they want Jensen back so bad? 

It’s simple: Jensen Huang’s value has nothing to do with GPUs or AI, and everything to do with keeping the AI bubble inflated.

Perhaps it’s more appropriate to call it the NVIDIA Bubble, because without it, the AI industry doesn’t really make much sense. 

As I’ll make clear later in this piece, NVIDIA played an active role in keeping the wheels of the AI bubble turning — funding model labs, buying startups, and backstopping compute for Neoclouds, thereby allowing them to raise debt. Its interventions didn’t merely sustain the industry-wide spending spree, but amplified it. In the process, NVIDIA transformed the AI bubble to something that attached itself to the personal wealth of ordinary people — often without them realizing it.  

As the stock prices of NVIDIA (and the rest of the Magnificent Seven) became engorged on AI-related hysteria, the exposure of ordinary (and unwitting) savers to the AI bubble grew. Investors who followed the mantra of “don’t buy individual stocks, just buy index funds” ended up in a position where, due to the top-heavy nature of the S&P 500, and the predominance of mega-cap tech stocks, a significant chunk of their wealth is gambled on the question of whether AI is a bubble or not. And that’s without mentioning other factors — like how insurers and pension funds are exposed to the AI bubble (and, in particular, the AI infrastructure buildout), either directly or indirectly through their investments in private credit. 

Or, put succinctly, if NVIDIA sneezes, the retirement savings and personal investments of ordinary retail investors will catch a cold. And if NVIDIA catches the flu, we’ll see the wealth of retail investors contract the fiscal equivalent of pneumonic plague — the type that Soviet scientists cooked up in a Siberian lab during the Cold War, and that gives Annie Jacobsen nightmares. 

Despite many saying “NVIDIA isn’t NVIDIA without Jensen,” in truth it’s still selling the same chips, has the same fab space and supplier agreements, and outside of his horrible personality (and cult of personality) seems virtually identical.

Back in August, NVIDIA said that it expected 70% year-over-year growth in Fiscal Year 2028 (starting February 2027), which suggests — unless something has materially changed! — that NVIDIA had clear expectations and agreements to hit those targets. CEO Colette Kress should, if you believe everything that’s been said over the last few years about “insatiable demand,” have absolutely no problem selling just as many GPUs at just as fast a rate…

…unless, of course, there’s another reason that “NVIDIA isn’t NVIDIA without Jensen.”

The truth is that what people actually mean is that “NVIDIA isn’t NVIDIA without Jensen using its balance sheet to grow at a high pace involving constant, quasi-legal-to-illegal dealmaking involving channel stuffing and illegal smuggling.”

The Wall Street Journal reports that Jensen Huang had told his finance team (in August, the very same month it raised guidance) that the company was facing a glut of GPUs and had over-ordered capacity at TSMC and with memory manufacturers, necessitating further circular financing:

When Nvidia used its creditworthy balance sheet to help OpenAI sign a massive data center lease in Piketon, Ohio, with SoftBank’s SB Energy, it cut the scale of its commitment in August during negotiations. Kress had become skeptical of the scale of the deal. 

Huang told his finance team in August that the company was under pressure, The Wall Street Journal previously reported. Major cloud providers were making plans to use alternative chips and lessen their reliance on the firm, and Nvidia was staring at a glut of chip wafers and memory it had committed to buying, he told them.

The then-CEO pressed staff to develop a way to decide whether guarantees were worthwhile. Later that month, it paused some deals in that initiative, the Journal reported.

I dunno man, I’m no securities lawyer, but I feel like worrying that you have an oversupply of chips and then telling investors that you actually expect to sell more chips than ever feels like some sort of stock manipulation, and it wouldn’t be the first time NVIDIA’s done it in the last year. Back in September 2025, it announced it would invest $100 billion in OpenAI to build 10GW of data center capacity, with Jensen Huang saying live on CNBC that there had “never been an engineering project of this complexity and this scale ever,” referring to a deal that he would dismiss as “never a commitment” five months later, because it was only ever a “letter of intent.”

The truth is that Jensen Huang lied. You can dress it up in terms of “memoranda of understanding” or “letters of intent” not actually meaning “a contract has been signed,” but Jensen Huang went on CNBC and did everything he could to convince you that NVIDIA was investing $100 billion in OpenAI to build 10GW of data centers, much like he went on CNBC a few months ago to convince you that (and I quote the headline) “NVIDIA [had lined] up $500 billion in financing” despite these being A) memoranda of understanding and B) no money ever changing hands or being raised by anybody to do anything and, to quote Bloomberg, said $500 billion figure having “no obvious provenance.”

There is no other way to interpret this other than intentional manipulation of the markets perpetuated by the mainstream business and technology press, all because nobody would ever push back on Jensen Huang. 

And that’s because everybody knows, deep down, that we’re all living in an NVIDIA Bubble — a financial mania manufactured, maintained and sustained using NVIDIA’s credit rating and cash to brute-force the markets and the media into believing in anything.

How Jensen Huang Created A One-Man Financial Mania Using NVIDIA’s Balance Sheet

My name is Jen-Hsun Huang, and for the last thirty-three years, I thought I was the one and only CEO of NVIDIA. I bought an Israeli networking company, sold some GPUs, got my buddy Satya to build a cluster, I saved the stock market, I made some circular deals — never invest in a former cryptocurrency miner — I tried to sell some GPUs to the Chinese, I helped out some of my buddies, all to keep the AI bubble alive…

While the AI bubble is relatively young, the NVIDIA bubble has been inflating for over a decade.

I don’t even mean that derisively! Jensen Huang and NVIDIA were formative to the entire AI bubble, both in creating the infrastructure, demand, and even the underlying research that eventually led to the LLM boom. 

Way back in August 2016, Jensen Huang delivered “the world’s first AI supercomputer” — the DGX-1 — to a small AI lab called OpenAI that had recently raised money from yCombinator’s Sam Altman and Tesla/SpaceX’s Elon Musk. Three months later, OpenAI announced it was moving to Microsoft Azure, training on NVIDIA Pascal GPUs in the earliest days of AI compute.

A few years later, NVIDIA found itself in flux, with a beat on earnings in February 2019 clouded by a decline in both hyperscale and cloud sales, but Jensen Huang was already working on an acquisition that would change everything, agreeing to buy Israeli high-speed networking firm Mellanox that March for $6.9 billion in cash, outbidding both Microsoft (which was already using its tech at Azure) and Intel for the InfiniBand technology that would eventually allow NVIDIA to network together clusters of AI servers. 

Four months later in July 2019, Microsoft would invest a billion dollars into OpenAI “...to build “new Azure AI supercomputing technologies.” Four months later in November 2019, NVIDIA and Microsoft would announce that Azure would now offer a “a new kind of GPU-accelerated supercomputer in the cloud on Microsoft Azure,” networking together up to 800 NVIDIA V100 GPUs using Mellanox’s InfiniBand tech, and the first time I can find where you could rent out massive clusters of AI GPUs. Microsoft and NVIDIA engineers even trained their own conversational AI model called BERT.

The deal itself wouldn’t close until April 2020, and a month later in May, Microsoft and OpenAI would announce that they had built a 10,000 GPU “supercomputer” together, with sources telling The Register that it was likely made up of AMD CPUs and NVIDIA V100 GPUs. 

The same month, NVIDIA would release its A100 GPUs, which remain somewhat of a workhorse for AI Compute, and were a huge commercial success. Another significant milestone came two months later in July 2020, when NVIDIA would publish a blog about how OpenAI researchers had released a paper describing how they’d trained GPT-3 using its Volta-era V100 GPUs (released in 2017). 

In August 2020, NVIDIA’s data center revenue would outpace its gaming revenue for the first time in the company’s history, “aided largely by the Mellanox acquisition” per Holger Mueller of Constellation Research. 

In other words, Jensen Huang and NVIDIA were far more foundational to the AI bubble than Sam Altman or Elon Musk, quite literally buying and building the company and the infrastructure necessary to build large language models. 

While June 2017’s Attention Is All You Need paper absolutely kicked off the transformer-based model boom, NVIDIA and Baidu’s late 2017 research into mixed precision training that allowed model developers to use nearly half as much memory during training without losing accuracy, and also train faster on NVIDIA’s newer chips, a technique that became the standard in the early days of LLMs, shouldn’t be overlooked.

In August 2021, OpenAI would launch Triton, a Python-esque coding language specifically built to make it easy to write code that ran on GPUs that would become foundational to the entire AI boom. Three months later, Microsoft announced that OpenAI’s GPT-3 was now available on an invite-only basis to customers via its new Azure OpenAI Service.

Then came 2022 — a rough year for everybody, per my second Hater’s Guide To NVIDIA: 

Microsoft’s FY2023 revenues only grew 6.9% year-over-year. NVIDIA’s FY2023 (which ran February 2022 to January 2023) was effectively flat, sitting at 0.2% as the post-pandemic surge of demand for gaming GPUs and networking gear puttered out, with Q4 2023 revenues dropping by 21% year-over-year. 

Meta, Google, and Amazon, all of which have fiscal years that align with the calendar year, saw growth deteriorate:

* Google went from 41.6% year-over-year growth in 2021 to 10.3% and 9.7% in 2022 and 2023.
* Meta went from 37.2% year-over-year growth in 2021 to negative 1.1% in 2022 and 15.7% in 2023.
* Amazon went from 37.6% year-over-year growth in 2020, to 21.7% in 2021, to 9.4% in 2022, to 1.8% in 2023 (and has really never recovered.)

NVIDIA’s Q3 FY23 (November 2022) earnings were rough, missing on analyst expectations, though not as rough as Q2 FY23, when it had to pre-announce that it had missed on guidance by a little under $2 billion. 

While NVIDIA had started shipping its H100 GPUs with data center sales eclipsing its gaming revenue by about $2.2 billion, it had yet to fill the hole caused by the post-pandemic dropoff of PC and graphics card sales or, more aptly, the hole left by the collapse of cryptocurrency mining. 

And then a mere two weeks later, Sam Altman announced the launch of ChatGPT, creating the greatest sense of FOMO in the tech industry’s history. Even with the best possible read of those annualized run rates, these startups raise hundreds of millions or billions of dollars’ worth of funding to make tens or hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue, and need to do so every few months due to the remarkable cost of renting NVIDIA GPUs, which despite being multiple generations in do not seem to be getting more efficient for the end customer.

In many ways Jensen Huang created the perfected form of Jack Welch’s GE Capital, manipulating the markets, the media and the banking system into affirming his every decision by making sure that everybody had somebody else to pay or get paid by, even if the entire system was terrifyingly brittle. 

And the worst part is that Jensen never really cared about whether there was demand for AI outside of its ability to justify further debt or cash for buying AI GPUs. The majority of the backstops that NVIDIA has provided — like its leases for Oracle, Anthropic, and OpenAI — require the data center capacity to be built before NVIDIA pays a dime, punting any theoretical time at which he or his heir would have to “backstop” anything into a time so far in the future that it doesn’t really matter. 

Every CoreWeave or neocloud debt deal follows the same path — a customer agrees to buy unbuilt capacity, the debt is raised, the GPUs are bought, and then nothing happens until the data center is actually finished, which may take years, but none of that matters as long as NVIDIA got paid.

Who knows what happens in NVIDIA’s earnings today. Perhaps they beat and raise again, with Colette Kress coasting off of the previous three months’ worth of circular financing deals that kept the machine alive. 

Then again, the amount of stories in the past week that have said something to the effect of “Colette Kress and NVIDIA do not want to do circular financing anymore” suggest that the company may be getting ahead of something — such as pulling or lowering revenue guidance, perhaps blaming everything on the “challenging transition” rather than “the collapse of the circular financing economy.”

In any case, the NVIDIA Bubble has popped. Jensen Huang is done. NVIDIA is no longer the circular financing titan, and anybody depending on its theoretical backing for future financing or funding is shit out of luck. There is no longer a well-funded boob-signing billionaire playboy left to beguile the press, con financiers, and pump the most wretched of bags in an endless conga-line of dodgy deals with goal of goosing NVIDIA’s revenues by any means necessary, even if the eventual data centers never actually get bought.

Sidenote: fair warning to anybody who attempts to retcon their (or their publication’s) coverage of circular financing, NVIDIA or the AI bubble in general: I have been saving stuff for years. Any attempts by boosters to backtrack will be met with force.

The NVIDIA Bubble inflated at the perfect time, with Jensen capitalizing on the industry-wide knowledge (as I wrote back in the Rot-Com Bubble) that tech was flat out of hypergrowth ideas. NVIDIA offered hyperscalers and their brainless executives a panacea — a magical chip that allowed them to monopolize both the software layer and the infrastructure underpinning it, if only they’d just buy enough GPUs and build enough data centers to house them. All that mattered to Jensen was keeping them believing in the dream.

Unfortunately, the vast majority of people do not want to pay for AI, and the vast majority of those who pay for AI compute can’t afford to do so. Those buying NVIDIA GPUs refuse to explain how much money they’re making from renting them out, or what it costs to do so. We do not know how many active AI GPUs there are in the world, and hyperscalers like Microsoft have taken great pains to mislead us into believing they have gigawatts more in capacity than they actually have. 

There’s a reason that NVIDIA has $36 billion in compute commitments — because the actual demand for AI compute is much, much smaller than the demand he created for his GPUs.

None of this mattered because Jensen Huang always made sure that nobody thought about it too much.

The moment NVIDIA’s growth slows, it’ll be all that anybody can think about.

title: Beyond Linux: A Journey Through the Open Source Ecosystem
content:
What follows is the text of the talk I gave at Linux Day 2026 in Modena, lightly adapted for the blog. The talk was in Italian, in front of a Linux audience - which explains a few of the jokes.

Linux is one of the best-known players in the open source world, but it's not the only possible path. A journey through the BSDs, illumos and other alternative operating systems, to reflect on Open Source as an idea, a philosophy and a practice of sharing knowledge.

My name is Stefano Marinelli. I'm a sysadmin and consultant, and I run my own small company specialised in open source services and solutions. I like to call myself the "Barista" of the BSD Cafe and the illumos Cafe, online communities of people passionate about technology, open source and sharing. Today I'm not here just to talk about operating systems, but about freedom, sharing and knowledge. From free software to open source.

My first contact with the Free Software world was in 1996, when I wasn't even 17 yet. I saw a box set advertised in a magazine: "a whole operating system, for free", at a very low price. Something like 30,000 lire. Shortly before, I'd paid roughly ten times as much for the Windows 95 upgrade edition. Dismissive and without a shred of trust, I decided to order it and give it a go. I mean: who would ever write something like that... and release the source code? But six CDs for 30,000 lire... let's try. Worst case, it'll be an experience.

It was love at first shell. That terminal opened up a whole universe, and to what I already knew (commercial licences, freeware, shareware) I added the concept of Free Software. But I didn't have enough hardware to run two operating systems, so I reinstalled Windows and put it all off. Still, I started thinking. Reflecting. Studying. In 1997 I got a new PC and started using Linux - or, as I was careful to say, GNU/Linux - for everything. Except games. For those, a small Windows partition survived, though not for long.

In 1998 I enrolled in Computer Science at the University of Bologna. Even back then, it was a faculty strongly oriented towards free software. Linux in the labs. I was one of the few who, in the first year, already knew what Free Software was (not free as in price, but...freedom!) and how to use the Linux workstations. That gave me a big advantage, especially from the second year onwards. Renzo Davoli was already pushing hard in that direction. I decided that would be my path. And so it was, and I started pushing too. Windows wasn't the "enemy" to me. The imposition was. Personally, I respect rules, but not impositions. Some people followed me, others watched from a distance. I didn't care. I was widening my horizons.

In the early 2000s I also discovered the BSDs. And I convinced my parents that I needed a laser printer for "university material". In reality, I wanted to print the excellent BSD documentation. Maybe not university material, but the printed FreeBSD Handbook probably served me better than half of the theory exams I took back then. Thanks, mom and dad!

But let's get back to the beginning.

Free Software was born out of a change. In those days, code circulated freely among people. Depending on their needs, they exchanged source code, modified it and shared it again. But at some point this began to change. There's an anecdote that, while not exhaustive, gives the idea: the printer Richard Stallman was using kept jamming, and nobody got notified. He wanted to modify the software so that he'd get a notification, as he'd done with the previous printer. Back then it was common practice, but this time he was refused. "I can't share the source code. It's under NDA." In other words, he had lost control over what he was using. He even wanted to improve the program, and instead he got a refusal.

The rest is history. At least until a few years ago.

Because thirty years ago we fought for Free Software to be taken seriously. When I started working, I was almost laughed at. "That's toy stuff you use at university. The real world uses something else." "Why don't you just use Windows? Everything's easier." And yet, the toys often worked better than the expensive proprietary solutions. Or at least just as well, at a fraction of the cost. "Let's try. Don't pay me until you're satisfied." They smiled, incredulous. Then they paid, happily. We could prove there was an alternative. Free, with no artificial locks. Something that anyone - even the broke but eager student - could study and set up. Technology, that kind of "enterprise" technology, was truly within everyone's reach. There was no need to buy expensive products, or recurring certifications just to have the "right" to work on them. You study, you apply yourself, nobody can stop you. I attended Linux Days. I spoke at Linux Days. For example, here I am, in Linux Day 2004.

We won that battle. We won that war. Linux - chaotic Linux, built by countless external contributors, made of different and varied distributions - has reached everywhere. Open Source is everywhere. But something happened - something beautiful, but terrible: precisely because it reached everywhere, something changed in the spirit. "Too big to fail". And so the big players arrived. Today, Linux development is driven by corporate money: companies like Microsoft (the same Microsoft that once considered Linux its sworn enemy - or Red Hat itself) and other big tech players. In itself, this has been a good thing. In practice, though, it means that they steer its development, even if indirectly. Year after year, it has started to take the shape of a different kind of product. Is the user still at the centre, or is it more code to make Azure run better? Sure, it's Open Source, it's free. But it's increasingly close to the needs of the big companies funding its development and, at times, further from the ordinary user. That's not necessarily bad: many of these investments have given us extraordinary technologies.

But I wonder whether, in the process, we're losing something. Not so much in the code as in the mindset. If not in the kernel, then in the community around it.

Back then, precisely because we were frustrated by "It only works on Windows", we were careful to write portable software. I'll say one word, without going into too much detail: POSIX. Once a mantra: POSIX compliant. A set of standards defining common interfaces between operating systems, so you can write programs that, with few or even no changes, run on different Unix and Unix-like systems. Today, in the communities around Linux, you hear more and more often that POSIX is "outdated". When I send a patch to make a specific tool work on FreeBSD, for example, I often read comments like: "Why don't you just use Linux?". And that déjà vu sends a shiver down my spine: is the community I loved so much turning into a copy, albeit a better one, of its worst enemy?

But careful: I'm not here to speak ill of Linux. That would be absurd. I mean: coming to Linux Day to trash Linux? It's an extraordinary operating system, and I owe it a great deal.

I'm here to remind you that Linux isn't the only way to understand free software. And that a project being less well known doesn't make it less interesting, less valid or less worthy of attention. Because if freedom of choice is truly a value, we must be ready to defend it even when someone chooses something different from what we choose.

So let's see what lies beyond Linux. Because monoculture is a problem, in Open Source too.

Because free software is...free. And we must be free too. Free to choose, to consider alternatives. To contribute, if we want to. To understand which solution best fits our problem. We don't have to pick a single solution "because everyone does". We don't have to turn one monopoly into another. Linux is great. It helps put bread on my table, so I'm a fan. But there are alternatives, other solutions, that can have their advantages. And that's why I want to talk to you about the BSDs and illumos.

The BSDs

BSD stands for Berkeley Software Distribution. And the first curious thing is that its story begins before Linux even existed. We're in the late Seventies. At the University of California, Berkeley, some researchers are working on UNIX, the operating system developed at AT&T's Bell Labs. They don't just use it. They modify it, improve it, write new programs and share that work with other universities.

Remind you of something? We've just been talking about Stallman and the culture of sharing.

BSD was born in exactly that world. So it was born on solid, stable, reliable foundations. Studied by experts, not as a game. BSD was an operating system directly related to Unix. It was a complete and stable system, but it wasn't yet available for "home" systems, the i386 family. Born well before Linux. A curiosity: Linus Torvalds himself, in a 1993 interview, said: "If 386BSD had been available when I started on Linux, Linux would probably never had happened.". Yes, you heard that right. Linus Torvalds said it. And we're at a Linux Day!

Then something happened: BSD arrived on the i386, and Unix System Laboratories, controlled by AT&T, started a rather insidious legal dispute: there's our code in BSD and you have no right to use, modify or share it. The University of California was dragged into it too. This was a real blocker for many. Companies were afraid to adopt an operating system with a lawsuit like that in progress. The matter dragged on until 1994, when a settlement was reached and 4.4BSD-Lite was released, with a freely redistributable and legally cleared base.

Meanwhile, Linux was growing, attracting developers, winning users. It didn't have that particular legal uncertainty. I'm not saying Linux succeeded only because of this. That would be unfair to Torvalds and to the thousands of people who contributed to its development.

But it's interesting to think that the history of computing as we know it could have taken a different path. And it's also interesting that, despite these difficulties, BSD didn't disappear. Quite the opposite.

From that story came some of the operating systems I want to talk about today. Systems that took different paths and that are still developed, used and improved. Different operating systems - careful, not distributions of the same operating system! - each unique in its own way. Let's start with FreeBSD.

FreeBSD

FreeBSD is probably the most general-purpose BSD. It's a complete operating system, designed to offer stability, performance and a certain consistency in administration. And here's a first difference from Linux I'd like to highlight. In the BSDs, the kernel and the userland, the base tools of the operating system, are developed and maintained within the same project. That doesn't mean Linux works worse. It means the development model is different.

And there's a philosophy I really appreciate: evolution, not revolution. It doesn't mean standing still. It means trying to improve without necessarily turning upside down what already works.

Let's talk about some technologies. ZFS, for example. An advanced filesystem, with snapshots, data integrity, replication and many other features. FreeBSD integrates it directly into the system and also lets you use Boot Environments: I can upgrade the system and, if something goes wrong, go back to the previous environment.

Then we have jails. FreeBSD has had a technology for isolating processes, resources and application environments since 2000. Long before Docker arrived. Jails aren't Docker, and I'm not saying they're the same thing. But they let you isolate applications and services simply, with low overhead, using the operating system's own features directly. A bit like LXC on Linux.

For virtualisation we have bhyve, which lets you run virtual machines, including other operating systems. And bhyve is lighter and, often, faster than KVM on Linux. [LINK: my bhyve articles]

But FreeBSD isn't just a system for enthusiasts. Netflix uses it to deliver video content. PlayStation consoles have a FreeBSD-derived base. macOS and iOS also include code from the BSD world. OPNsense and pfSense, two well-known firewall solutions, are based on FreeBSD. In short, we're not talking about a university toy. Remind you of something?

Personally, I've been using FreeBSD for many years, in production too. And it has often let me solve problems simply, while staying in control of what's happening. I've seen cases where, on the same hardware and with the same workload, FreeBSD handled I/O pressure better, with even very significant reductions in execution time. If you're curious, there are several articles about it here on IT Notes. That doesn't mean FreeBSD is always faster than Linux. That would be nonsense. It means there are situations where it can be the better choice.

And for me, this is the point: I solve problems. I don't have to defend an operating system. I have to pick the right tool.

OpenBSD

Then there's OpenBSD. OpenBSD was born in 1995 as a fork of NetBSD and is probably one of the most interesting systems when we talk about security and code correctness.

Its philosophy is fairly simple: less complexity, fewer chances for mistakes. The code is continuously reviewed, cleaned up, simplified. Features aren't added just because they might be interesting. Every choice has to make sense within the project. Because the more complex code becomes, the harder it is to maintain, audit and verify.

OpenBSD has also developed some very interesting security mechanisms, like pledge() and unveil(), which let you restrict the operations a program can perform and the parts of the filesystem it can access.

And then there's OpenSSH. Yes, the very OpenSSH you probably use every day to manage your servers. It was born, and is developed, within the OpenBSD project.

But there's another feature I love: the documentation. In the OpenBSD world, insufficient or wrong documentation is considered a bug. The man pages are often enough to understand how to use and configure the system, without hunting for guides of dubious quality scattered across the Internet. And believe me, when you manage dozens or hundreds of systems, knowing where to find correct and consistent information is a huge advantage.

OpenBSD doesn't try to please everyone. The developers follow their own priorities, even when that means giving up something other systems offer. Can it be frustrating? Certainly. But it also offers a great advantage: consistency, predictability and a clear design direction.

For firewalls, routers and systems where security is particularly important, it's an alternative always worth considering.

NetBSD

NetBSD, on the other hand, has a wonderful motto. "Of course it runs NetBSD!" And that already says a lot about its philosophy.

NetBSD puts a huge emphasis on portability, correctness of implementation and the ability to run on very different hardware architectures. Not just modern x86 or ARM computers. We're also talking about machines decades old, architectures many consider long forgotten. And careful: it's not just a matter of computing nostalgia.

Keeping an operating system working on such different platforms forces you to write code with great attention to portability, avoiding needless dependencies on a specific architecture.

Remember when, a moment ago, I was talking about POSIX and portability as a value? Well, NetBSD is one of the best examples of that philosophy. Because a system that can run on very different hardware must necessarily care about how correct, clean and portable its code is. And that has positive consequences on the more common platforms too.

There's another aspect I appreciate: continuity. We don't always need the latest novelty, the latest feature, the latest framework. Some devices and applications simply need to keep working, maybe for many years. Think of embedded systems, small computers, hardware that isn't replaced every two years. In these contexts, knowing there's a project that considers portability and support for different architectures a fundamental part of its identity is reassuring.

It's a different philosophy from FreeBSD's and from OpenBSD's. And that's absolutely fine.

NetBSD has also taken a clear stance on AI-generated code: it can't be committed without prior written approval, because it's considered potentially "tainted" - both in form and in licence. And in today's extremely polarised world, that's a sigh of relief for anyone who wants to use and develop an operating system without the pressure of always having to do more, add more features and more code.

The BSD Family

There's also DragonFlyBSD, born in 2003 as a fork of FreeBSD, which followed other design choices, especially regarding the kernel and system management. We don't have time to go into everything, but I want to stress one thing. These systems have common origins and share part of their history, but they don't necessarily have the same goals.

FreeBSD is a general-purpose system, also oriented towards performance and production environments. It's stable and secure. On the desktop it might not support all the hardware Linux does, although they're working on it. But on servers it could be one of the best alternatives to Linux.

OpenBSD favours security, simplicity and code correctness. NetBSD focuses heavily on portability and on supporting different hardware. DragonFlyBSD has experimented with other architectural solutions. And yet, they all belong to the big BSD family.

There's no need for one to win over the others. It's not a battle. There's nothing to sell here. It's freedom. It's diversity. And that diversity is a strength.

If there's one thing I've learnt over all these years, it's exactly this: an operating system shouldn't be a religion. In my daily life, I solve problems. And to solve them, I need to be able to evaluate the alternatives.

Because stability, for example, isn't just a system's ability not to crash. It's also being able to update it without surprises, to understand how it works, to know what happens when something goes wrong. Observability is fundamental, and being able to have it without weaving together fifty Docker containers can sometimes make the difference between ten minutes of work and two hours.

We don't always need to reinvent everything. What's new isn't always better. And the solution chosen by the majority isn't always the best fit for our problem. Often, it's exactly the opposite.

But our journey doesn't end with the BSDs.

illumos

There's another family of operating systems that descends from a different UNIX history. A history that runs through Sun Microsystems, Solaris and OpenSolaris. And that leads us to illumos.

Now someone might ask: weren't you talking about the BSDs? Yes, but the talk is called Beyond Linux, not Only BSD!

illumos isn't a BSD. It descends from another branch of the big UNIX family. The Solaris one, developed by Sun Microsystems. Sun. Anyone remember it? SPARC workstations, servers, Solaris, Java. In the Nineties and the 2000s it was one of the biggest names in professional computing.

And Solaris was a very interesting operating system. Designed for serious machines, serious workloads, situations where a problem could cost a lot. In Bologna, when I was a student, there were some Solaris machines in the UnderLab. I looked at them sideways. To me they were "non-Linux". So I didn't like them.

In 2005 Sun did something significant: it started publishing the Solaris source code through the OpenSolaris project. Imagine: a commercial UNIX system, with years of development behind it, advanced technologies and long experience in enterprise environments, opening up to the community. It wasn't the first free software to be used in companies, of course. But it was another way of doing things. Another model.

And then, in 2010, Oracle acquired Sun. And here things changed. Oracle decided to stop the open development of OpenSolaris and stopped publishing new code updates.

End of the story?

No.

Because the code that had already been released under an open source licence remained available. Oracle could decide not to publish its developments any more, but it couldn't take back the freedoms already granted on that code. And that's how illumos was born. A group of developers decided to carry on the work, starting from the open OpenSolaris base.

Think about it for a moment. A company acquires another company, changes strategy and stops the public development of an operating system. But that system doesn't die. Because the code exists, the skills exist, and there are people willing to keep working on it.

Remind you of something? We began this talk with Stallman and a printer whose code couldn't be shared. Thirty years later, the very possibility of sharing and modifying code allows a whole family of operating systems to keep existing.

This, for me, is one of the most beautiful aspects of free software.

But let's get back to the technology. Because illumos isn't just a nice story.

The technologies and distributions of illumos

From Solaris, illumos inherited some extremely interesting technologies. You already know one: ZFS. ZFS was born at Sun. It's a filesystem, but also a volume manager. It lets you manage storage, snapshots, data replication, integrity checks and much more.

I use ZFS practically everywhere I can. On FreeBSD, on illumos, on NetBSD and on Linux too. And that's already an example of how a good technology can cross different operating systems.

Then we have DTrace. DTrace lets you observe what's happening inside a system, even while it's running. We can analyse kernel calls, processes, performance, behaviours that would otherwise be hard to understand. For a sysadmin, it's an extraordinary tool. Because when a client tells you "the server is slow", the problem isn't knowing it's slow. They already know that. The problem is understanding why.

Then there are Zones. An isolation system that lets you run separate environments sharing the same kernel. Remember FreeBSD's jails? Well, zones were inspired by FreeBSD's jails. The concept is similar, although the implementations and some features differ.

And then Crossbow, for network virtualisation. SMF, for managing services and their dependencies. In short, we're talking about a system with important technologies, born to tackle concrete problems. Not an experiment cobbled together in someone's spare time. And careful, I'm not saying these technologies are necessarily better than those available on Linux or the BSDs. I'm saying they're different, they have their own history and, in certain contexts, they can be particularly useful.

Like Linux, illumos is the base of several distributions, each with different features and goals.

SmartOS, for example, is focused on virtualisation. It has an interesting peculiarity: the operating system is loaded into RAM, from USB or from the network (or even from the local disk, but then it runs read-only), leaving the disks to the virtual machines and the data, managed with ZFS. It supports native Zones, LX zones to run Linux applications, and virtual machines via KVM and bhyve. Yes, the very bhyve we've already met talking about FreeBSD! Personally, I'm using and experimenting with it a lot. It's not all roses, but I really like some of its solutions. And bhyve on illumos even has a few gems that haven't been brought back to FreeBSD. Open Source and collaboration between projects, at their best!

OmniOS takes a more traditional road. It's an operating system designed mainly for servers, with particular attention to stability, updates and long-term continuity. It offers stable releases and long-term support versions. You install it, configure your services and use it. Without necessarily having to reinvent everything at every update.

OpenIndiana is perhaps the closest to the classic idea of a general-purpose UNIX distribution. It can be used on servers, but also as a desktop system, with a full graphical environment. For anyone who'd like to try a Solaris-derived system on their own computer, it could be an interesting starting point.

And then there's Tribblix, a rather special project. Created by Peter Tribble, it combines an almost nostalgic, traditional UNIX feel with modern components. It has its own package management system and a modular approach through overlays, which let you install groups of software. A small, independent system with a very precise personality.

Four distributions sharing a technological base, but interpreting it in different ways. Remind you of something? Linux... And that's exactly the point. There's no single way to build an operating system. There's no single development philosophy.

And none of them needs to prevail over the others. What matters is that they keep existing, evolving and offering alternatives. Because, in the end, freedom of choice only has value if we really have something to choose from.

So, why illumos if we already have Linux and the BSDs?

Because there's a whole UNIX tradition that isn't Linux and isn't BSD. Because some technologies now considered fundamental in modern computing were born right there. And, still today, they're stable and reliable. They're refined and polished without being "rewritten" or replaced every five years because there's a new fashion. Because we can use systems that followed different paths, with different architectures and design choices.

But above all, because illumos is also a practical demonstration of the value of free software. Sun opened the code. Oracle decided to stop that open development. The community was able to carry on.

It wasn't easy, and it doesn't mean every open source project can automatically survive the disappearance of whoever was funding it. You need developers, resources, skills. You need someone willing to take care of it. Available code is a necessary condition, but on its own it isn't enough.

And this brings us to a point that, for me, is fundamental. Free software isn't just code. It's also the people who choose to develop it, maintain it, document it and share it.

That's why, alongside the BSD Cafe, I also wanted to create the illumos Cafe. To offer a space to meet, discuss and share experiences about technologies that maybe don't make the front pages of tech sites every day.

Because we don't all have to use the same operating system. We don't even all have to agree. But we can learn something from each other. And maybe discover a solution to a problem we didn't even know we could tackle differently.

Careful, though. I'm not saying the BSD or illumos communities are better than the Linux ones. In our world too there's fundamentalism, prejudice, and people who consider their own choice the only possible one. And that's a problem too. Because it makes no sense to defend software freedom and then look down on someone who decides to use a system different from ours.

We don't all have to agree. In fact, it would be terribly boring. We must be able to disagree, compare ideas, learn something and keep respecting each other - even in disagreement - while building something constructive. What matters, in the end, is being able to choose. And that's true freedom.

More than twenty years ago, at Linux Days, I talked about how Linux could replace Windows in many areas, both on the desktop and on servers. That it was a valid alternative. Today I'm here to tell you not to let yourselves be chained by habit. Linux/Docker/Kubernetes is an exceptional combination, but not the only one. It would be serious if it were, because we'd have lost our freedom. The freedom to publish an Open Source project as a tarball of source code instead of putting it "on GitHub" or similar.

Open source is not about doing things the approved way. It is about giving people the freedom to do things another way.

Open Source and Closed Minds never get along.

Stay free. Always.
